items.label: Virtue moment
items.what: A short story, verse or conversation about the term's virtue, and the habit chart.

sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: The outline calls Virtue Formation "not a course" but a framework that runs through every course, and the answer to the question of what all this learning is for (§3J). It names the seven classical virtues: the four cardinal virtues, inherited from Plato and Aristotle and taken up by Aquinas, and the three theological virtues from 1 Corinthians 13.

Its central caution shapes everything here: virtue is formed by practice and imitation, not by instruction. It cannot be assessed with a quiz, and any attempt to score it will corrupt it. The platform tracks that a virtue term happened and what the family did; it never produces a virtue grade (§3J).
So this course has very little "lesson" in it. Each term it gives the family four things (§3J): a Scripture passage, a story, a practical habit, and an honest conversation.
As the outline puts them to a child (§3J).

head: Virtue
Latin
Put to a child
rows: Think before you act. Know the right thing to do, and know how to do it.
Give every person what he is owed. Be fair when no one is watching.
Do the right thing when it costs you. Keep going when it is hard.
Govern yourself. Vincit qui se vincit: he conquers who conquers himself.
Trust God, and be someone others can trust.
Expect good, and work toward it, even in a hard season.
Love, and act on it. Put another's good ahead of your own.

blocks.text: The Latin names come from the language the child is learning this year (Latin I, 09).

One virtue per six-week term, with Faith and Hope paired in Term 1 so that seven virtues fit six terms. The year opens with faith and hope and closes with charity, following 1 Corinthians 13:13: "faith, hope, and love remain… The greatest of these is love."

The habits for Terms 2 and 4 are the outline's own examples (§3J). The others follow the same pattern: small, concrete, observable at home.
Very lightly, by design. About five minutes a week, plus the habit itself.

head: Week
What happens
rows: Introduce the virtue: its name in English and Latin, what it means put to a child, and the Scripture verse. Add the verse to the Memory Work box. Start the habit.
One short virtue moment a week, at a meal or bedtime: tell or retell the term's story, or point to where the virtue showed up in another course that week. Keep the habit going.
The honest conversation: how did the habit go? What was hard? Where did we see this virtue? What will we keep? Not a grade.

blocks.text: The term manuals give each week's story moment and the week 6 conversation questions.

sections.title: 5. Where it lives in the day

blocks.text: Virtue Formation has no time slot of its own. It is carried by:
The daily core: the verse is in the Memory Work box; the story moments often fit after Bible.
The content courses: Literature, History and Bible supply the stories; each of their term manuals already names the virtue of the term.

Physical Education and the practical arts: where the virtues become real (§3J): fortitude on a cold-morning hike, temperance in saving rather than spending, charity in a service project, justice in how a team treats its weakest member.
Home life: the habit is kept at home, in ordinary days.

sections.title: 6. What is recorded, and what isn't

blocks.text: Recorded (for the family and the platform):
That the virtue term happened.
The habit the family chose, and whether it was kept most days (a simple chart of marks, like Franklin's).
A sentence or two from the week 6 conversation, if the family wishes.
Never recorded: a score, a grade, a rating of the child's character, or any comparison between children. That's the outline's firm line (§3J).

head: Course
Link
rows: A virtue story each term; each Literature term manual names the virtue
Real examples from the period: Valley Forge, the Convention, Lewis and Clark
The Scripture verses, and Bible stories for each virtue; Term 6's 1 Corinthians 13 is also Bible's memory passage
Each term's verse goes into the box in week 1
The Latin names of the virtues; Ōrā et labōrā and Vēritās vōs līberābit touch faith and justice
Each PE term names the virtue in small, practical ways
Fable morals often name a virtue; a parent may point it out
Fortitude, temperance and charity in real work (§3J)

blocks.text: A missed week costs nothing. Virtue isn't on a schedule; pick up at the next moment.
A habit that isn't working can be changed mid-term for a smaller one. The aim is a habit actually kept, not a hard one abandoned.
Never make up "missed virtue". If a term is disrupted, simply have the week 6 conversation and move on.

sections.title: 9. What each term manual will contain

blocks.text: The virtue in English and Latin, and what it means put to a child; the Scripture verse in full; the term's stories, with where to find them in the other courses; the six-week habit, with a simple marks chart; a short "virtue moment" for each of weeks 2–5; and the week 6 honest-conversation questions.

head: Latin
Put to a child
rows: Trust God, and be someone others can trust.
Expect good, and work toward it, even in a hard season.

blocks.text: This term pairs two virtues so that all seven fit into the year. They belong together: faith trusts God's promises, and hope looks forward to them. Weeks 1–3 lean on faith; weeks 4–6 on hope.
Hebrews 11:1, World English Bible.
Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen.
Words to explain: assurance (being sure) · proof (something that shows a thing is true). Put simply: faith is being sure of what we hope for, even before we can see it.
Add the verse to the Memory Work box in week 1.

A short prayer said by the child each day, at a set time: morning, a meal or bedtime. Any words are fine. And once a week, one hope written on a "hope page": something good the child is looking forward to or working toward.
Mark the chart below each day the prayer is said. Marks only: no stars, prizes or scores.
Introduce faith and hope. Say the two names, in English and Latin, and what each means put to a child. Read Hebrews 11:1. Start the habit and the hope page.

The Pilgrims. They left their homes and crossed the ocean to worship God as they believed was right. They trusted God with a journey into the unknown. (Bible's church history, week 2; Literature and History meet the Pilgrims this term.)
Noah. God told Noah to build an ark before any rain came. Noah built it. (Bible, week 3.) Ask: why was that faith?
Abraham and the stars. God promised Abraham descendants as many as the stars, and Abraham believed him. That promise was something to hope for. (Bible, week 4.) This week, turn toward hope.
Sarah Noble. Alone in the woods at night, she remembered her mother's words: "Keep up your courage, Sarah Noble." (Literature, weeks 1–5.) Hope is holding on in a hard place.
The honest conversation (below).
A quiet talk, not a test. Some questions to choose from:
1. How did the daily prayer go? Were there days it was hard to remember?
2. What did you write on your hope page? Is anything on it closer than it was?
3. Who did we hear about this term who trusted God? Who kept hoping?
4. When is it hard to trust? When is it hard to keep hoping?
5. What would you like to keep doing?

after.title: Record (for the family and the platform)

head: Virtue term held
yes
rows: From the conversation (optional, a sentence or two)

blocks.text: Never a grade, a score or a comparison (plan §6).
Model it. A child who sees a parent pray each day learns more than any lesson can teach.
Keep the hope page. At the end of the year it's a record of what the child looked forward to, and often of hopes fulfilled.

head: Latin
Put to a child
rows: Govern yourself. Vincit qui se vincit: he conquers who conquers himself.

blocks.text: Temperance is self-control: enough and not too much, finishing before starting, waiting instead of grabbing. Benjamin Franklin, whom the child meets in Literature this term, put temperance first on his list of virtues.
Proverbs 16:32, Brenton's Septuagint.
A man slow to anger is better than a strong man; and he that governs his temper better than he that takes a city.
Words to explain: slow to anger (not quick to get cross) · governs his temper (stays in control of his feelings) · takes a city (wins a battle). Ruling yourself is greater than conquering a city.
Add the verse to the Memory Work box in week 7.
Finish one task before starting another. This is the outline's own example (§3J). A game put away before the next one comes out; one job finished before the child moves on.
Keep it on a Franklin-style chart: Franklin made a small mark each day he kept his virtue. Do the same: one mark for each day the habit was kept. No scores, no prizes.
Introduce temperance: the name in English and Latin, the motto Vincit qui se vincit, and Proverbs 16:32. Start the habit and the chart.
The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse. The country mouse chose a simple meal in peace over a rich one in fear. (Literature's fable, week 8.) Ask: what does "enough" mean?
The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs. The farmer wanted all the gold at once and lost everything. (Literature, week 9.) Greed is the opposite of temperance.

Franklin's chart. As a young man Franklin wrote a list of virtues, with temperance first, and marked a chart each day to check himself. (Literature, Term 2.) Show the child that their own chart is the same idea.
The manna. In the wilderness, God told the people to gather only what they needed each day. Those who took too much found it spoiled. (Bible, week 9.)
The honest conversation (below).
1. How did "finish before you start" go? Look at the chart together.
2. When was it hardest to wait, or to stop?
3. Which story this term showed someone taking too much? Someone content with enough?
4. What does Vincit qui se vincit mean to you now?
5. What would you like to keep doing?

after.title: Record (for the family and the platform)

head: Virtue term held
yes
rows: Finish one task before starting another

blocks.text: Never a grade, a score or a comparison (plan §6).
Small and concrete. "Put the blocks away before the paints come out" is temperance a child can do.
Physical Education link: taking turns and resting before getting worn out are temperance on the field (PE Term 2).
Keep the Term 1 habit if it's going well. The new habit adds to it; it doesn't replace it.

head: Latin
Put to a child
rows: Do the right thing when it costs you. Keep going when it is hard.

blocks.text: Fortitude is courage and endurance together: facing what is frightening, and not giving up on what is hard. The outline itself names this term's best example: Washington at Valley Forge (§3J), which History and Literature both read this term.
Joshua 1:9, Brenton's Septuagint.
Lo! I have commanded thee; be strong and courageous, be not cowardly nor fearful, for the Lord thy God is with thee in all places whither thou goest.

Words to explain: lo (look!) · courageous (brave) · cowardly (running from what's right because you're afraid) · whither thou goest (wherever you go). (The child heard this verse in Bible Term 2, week 11.)
Add the verse to the Memory Work box in week 13.
Do the hardest task of the day first, without complaining. The child chooses the task each morning (a page of Arithmetic, a chore, a practice), and does it before anything easier.
Mark the chart each day it's done. Marks only.
Introduce fortitude: the name in English and Latin, what it means put to a child, and Joshua 1:9. Start the habit.
Paul Revere's ride. Revere rode out at night, knowing he might be caught. (Literature, weeks 13–15; History, week 15.)
David and Goliath. A shepherd boy faced a giant with a sling and five stones, trusting God. (Bible, week 15.)
Valley Forge. Washington's army spent a terrible winter at Valley Forge, cold and hungry, and didn't give up. (History, week 16; Literature, week 16.)
Crossing the Delaware. On a freezing Christmas night Washington led his army across the icy river. (Literature, week 17.) Ask: what made it hard? Why did they go on?
The honest conversation (below).
1. How did "hardest task first" go? Look at the chart together.
2. Which hard task got easier as the weeks went on?
3. Who in this term's stories kept going when it was hard?
4. When do you most need fortitude?
5. What would you like to keep doing?

after.title: Record (for the family and the platform)

blocks.text: Never a grade, a score or a comparison (plan §6).
Fortitude in small things. A third-grader's fortitude is finishing the hard page, going out on the cold morning, trying the cartwheel again. Notice it out loud.
Physical Education link: winter walks and tumbling practice (PE Term 3) are fortitude in action.
Christmas break. The habit can rest over the holiday; pick it back up when school does.

head: Latin
Put to a child
rows: Give every person what he is owed. Be fair when no one is watching.

blocks.text: Justice is giving each person their due: fairness, honesty, keeping your word, doing your share. This term History and Literature follow the men who wrote the Constitution, trying to make laws fair to large and small states alike.
Micah 6:8, Brenton's Septuagint.
Has it not been told thee, O man, what is good? or what does the Lord require of thee, but to do justice, and love mercy, and be ready to walk with the Lord thy God?
Words to explain: require (ask of you, expect) · do justice (do what is fair and right) · mercy (kindness to someone who needs it).
Add the verse to the Memory Work box in week 19.

Do a sibling's chore (or a parent's) without being asked, and without telling anyone. This is the outline's own example (§3J): justice when no one is watching. Only children can do a parent's chore, or a small job for a neighbor.
The child makes the mark on the chart, privately, each day they do it. The parent doesn't check up. That's the point.
Introduce justice: the name in English and Latin, what it means put to a child, and Micah 6:8. Start the habit.
The Commandments. "Thou shalt not steal", "Thou shalt not bear false witness": giving others what is theirs, including the truth. (Bible's catechism, Terms 3–4.)
A fair plan for everyone. At the Constitutional Convention, large and small states each wanted their way. They agreed on a plan that was fair to both. (History, week 20; Literature, weeks 22–23.)
Daniel. Daniel kept praying, even when the law said he mustn't, and was thrown to the lions. The king saw that Daniel had done no wrong. (Bible, week 22.)
Esther. Queen Esther went before the king, at risk to herself, to speak for her people. (Bible, week 23.) Ask: whom did Esther stand up for?
The honest conversation (below).
1. Did anyone notice the chores you did? Did it matter that they didn't?
2. Why is it harder to be fair when no one is watching?
3. Who in this term's stories did what was right, or fair, when it cost them?
4. What does "give every person what he is owed" mean at home? At play?
5. What would you like to keep doing?

after.title: Habit chart (the child marks it, privately)
Record (for the family and the platform)

head: Virtue term held
yes
rows: A chore done secretly for someone else

blocks.text: Never a grade, a score or a comparison (plan §6).
Let the secret stay secret. If you notice a chore done, say nothing, or a quiet thank-you at most. Praise in public turns justice into a show.
Physical Education link: fair play, honest counting and giving everyone a turn (PE Term 4).

head: Latin
Put to a child
rows: Think before you act. Know the right thing to do, and know how to do it.

blocks.text: Prudence is practical wisdom: stopping to think, planning ahead, and choosing well. This term History and Literature follow Lewis and Clark, who planned and packed for a journey no one had made before.
James 1:5, World English Bible.
But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
Words to explain: lacks (doesn't have enough of) · liberally (generously, freely) · without reproach (without scolding). If you don't know what to do, you can ask God for wisdom.
Add the verse to the Memory Work box in week 25.

Each evening, plan tomorrow. Lay out what's needed (clothes, books, shoes) and say the plan for the next day in one sentence: "Tomorrow I'll do Latin first, then help with lunch." It's thinking before acting, made into a daily practice.
Mark the chart each evening it's done. Marks only.
Introduce prudence: the name in English and Latin, what it means put to a child, and James 1:5. Start the habit.
Lewis and Clark prepare. Before setting out, they gathered supplies, tools, medicines and gifts, and chose their men with care, because they didn't know what lay ahead. (History, week 26.)
The wise and foolish builders. Read Matthew 7:24–27 together: one man built his house on rock and one on sand, and the storm came. Ask: which builder thought ahead?
Johnny Appleseed. John Chapman planted orchards ahead of the settlers, so that apple trees would be growing when the families arrived. (Literature, weeks 25–26.)

The Fox and the Cat. The fox boasted of a hundred tricks; the cat knew one, climbing a tree, and it saved her when the hounds came. (Literature's fable, week 28.) One good plan beats many clever ones.
The honest conversation (below).
1. How did planning tomorrow go? Did the plan help the next day?
2. Tell about a time this term you stopped to think before you acted.
3. Who in this term's stories planned well? Who didn't?
4. When you don't know the right thing to do, what can you do? (James 1:5.)
5. What would you like to keep doing?

after.title: Record (for the family and the platform)

blocks.text: Never a grade, a score or a comparison (plan §6).
Keep the plan tiny. One sentence and a pile of tomorrow's things is enough. The habit is the thinking, not the list.
Physical Education link: looking before throwing, deciding whether to run for the next base (PE Term 5).

head: Latin
Put to a child
rows: Love, and act on it. Put another's good ahead of your own.

blocks.text: Charity is love in action: not only feeling kindly, but doing good for others, especially when it costs us something. The year began with faith and hope; it ends with charity, "the greatest of these".
1 Corinthians 13:13, World English Bible.
But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love.

Words to explain: remain (last, stay forever). This verse joins the whole year: Term 1's faith and hope, and this term's love. (The child is memorizing 1 Corinthians 13:4–8a in Bible this term; this verse comes a few lines later in the same chapter.)
Add the verse to the Memory Work box in week 31.

subs.title: Ideas for the family service project

blocks.text: Bake or cook for a neighbor, a new family or someone who is ill.
Visit an elderly neighbor or relative, and bring a drawing or a song.
Collect food or clothing for those in need, through church or a local charity.
Help with a job at church: setting up, cleaning, gardening.
Write and send cards to people who might be lonely.
(The practical-arts tracks can help: a meal from the Hearth, a repair from the Workshop.)
One quiet kindness each day: help someone without being asked, share something, write a note, make a sibling's bed. And one family service project during the term (below).
Mark the chart each day a kindness is done. Marks only.
Introduce charity: the name in English and Latin, what it means put to a child, and 1 Corinthians 13:13. Start the habit, and choose the service project together.
The good Samaritan. A traveler was hurt and left on the road; two people passed by, but a Samaritan stopped, cared for him and paid for his keep. (Bible, Term 5, week 28.) Ask: who was the neighbor?
Plan or do the service project. Talk about who it's for and why.
The first Christians. They shared everything they had, so that no one among them was in need. (Bible, week 34.)
"With charity for all." Abraham Lincoln asked the country to act "with malice toward none, with charity for all." (Literature, Term 6.) Ask: what does charity for all look like at home?
The honest conversation (below), and a look back over the whole year.
1. What kindness are you most glad you did this term?
2. How did the service project go? How do you think the people we helped felt?
3. Who in this year's stories showed charity?
4. Why do you think charity is called "the greatest"?
5. Looking back over the year: which of the seven virtues was hardest for you? Which habit will you keep?
